transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-27 13:30 UTC
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Malhotra (Redwood SE), Evelyn Park (Head of ML, Lunaris), Marcus Chen (Platform Eng), Sofia Ruiz (PM)

Auto-generated summary (may be imperfect): Quick review of internal bench numbers; caching showed 30-40% token cost savings on happy-path; batching increased throughput but added tail latency; next steps: 24h run, share sheet.

Topics: cost/unit econ, tokens/sec per $, caching hit-rate, batching latency tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted unit economics, sample prompt distribution.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: hey everyone, thanks for hopping on, should we do quick roll call?
[00:06] Evelyn Park: yes hi, evelyn here, sorry doing two things, but I'm here.
[00:09] Marcus Chen: Marcus, platform.
[00:11] Sofia Ruiz: Sofia — product.
[00:13] Jordan Lee: great, priya from our infra team is here as well. Priya, want to kick us off with the bench summary?
[00:18] Priya Malhotra: yeah sure, quick tl;dr — we ran the 10k request sample you sent with current prompt distribution and got these rough numbers: hosted baseline (no cache, batch size 1) around 420 tokens/sec across our small pool, tokens per dollar roughly 1.8M tokens per $1 on that profile, with model A (fp16). with basic batching (adaptive up to 8) we saw throughput improve to about 850 tokens/sec but p95 latency increased from ~120ms to ~280ms in spikes, so there's a tail tradeoff.
[00:50] Evelyn Park: wait 1.8M tokens per dollar, that's the hosted? that seems... can you repeat?
[00:55] Priya Malhotra: yeah that's hosted baseline numbers from our instrumented run, approximations — it's sensitive to sequence length; your average seq was about 220 tokens.
[01:02] Marcus Chen: and the batching to 8 bumped throughput to 850 but p99 got worse? you said p95 280ms, p99?
[01:07] Priya Malhotra: p99 was around 650ms in the worst bursts, but median stayed low. so for real-time UI use-cases you might see a few slow responses on heavier tails.
[01:16] Sofia Ruiz: ok that matches what we saw in earlier integration — a couple of slow responses, users noticed.
[01:21] Jordan Lee: can you talk about caching results? that's big for their bill right?
[01:25] Priya Malhotra: sure — when we enabled prefix/KV caching (we simulated a 40% hit rate based on your sample set where many prompts share a common prefix), effective tokens generated decreased and we saw token-cost drop by ~32% on median. end-to-end tokens/sec per $ improved to about 2.6M tokens per $1 equivalently. caveat: hit-rate matters a lot — at 20% hit the savings fall to ~15%.
[01:52] Evelyn Park: 40% hit rate seems optimistic, our team thinks for our conversational flows maybe 25-30%? We do have a lot of repeated system prompts though.
[02:01] Priya Malhotra: totally — that's why we asked for more prompt distribution; small differences change the numbers materially.
[02:06] Marcus Chen: what about cold-starts and KV cache fill — do you have warm-up numbers?
[02:11] Priya Malhotra: we did a warm-up phase; initial 5 minutes hit-rate was low, then it climbed to that 40% in our sim. in production you'd want a pre-warm or seed cache if you have predictable prefixes.
[02:21] Jordan Lee: also worth noting you can combine caching with batching but there's a compounding effect on latency, right?
[02:27] Priya Malhotra: exactly — batching pulls together requests which helps throughput but can delay a cached response slightly because request waits for batch window. we saw average latency still acceptable, but if you need hard SLOs on p95 under 200ms, you may want lower batch windows or hybrid routing (fast lane for low-latency calls).
[02:42] Evelyn Park: what about dedicated capacity — you mentioned earlier that dedicated pools change unit econ?
[02:46] Jordan Lee: yes, we put the rough numbers in the pricing sheet. for POCs, hosted is simplest, but dedicated reserved capacity reduces unit cost roughly 15-25% depending on commit and model variant — because you amortize GPU cost and can use larger batch/compilation optimizations.
[02:59] Marcus Chen: is that assuming fixed 24/7 utilization? our traffic is more spiky.
[03:03] Jordan Lee: good point — dedicated shows best value when utilization is high or you can burst. we also offer mixed policies — reserved base with burst to hosted. that keeps committed cost lower with fallback.
[03:14] Sofia Ruiz: can you summarize the numbers again — tokens/sec/$ with cache vs without?
[03:18] Priya Malhotra: without cache baseline approx 1.8M tokens/$; with cache (40% hit) approx 2.6M tokens/$; with batching aggressive (but no cache) throughput 850 tokens/sec but cost per token doesn't change much — the cost per token improves slightly because of GPU efficiency maybe 5-8% better; biggest wins are cache + quantization.
[03:40] Evelyn Park: quantization — did you test int8 or 4-bit? how stable is quality?
[03:44] Priya Malhotra: we did a quick int8 emulation and a 4-bit quantized trace; quality profile depends on model — with our open model candidate, int8 had negligible quality delta on your eval set, 4-bit started to show slight hallucination uptick in long-form scenarios. we recommend int8 for now for cost safety.
[04:03] Marcus Chen: can Redwood's runtime automatically pick kernels for quantized paths?
[04:07] Priya Malhotra: yes that's one of the runtime pieces — compilation + kernel selection picks the best path based on model and sequences; you'll get the best perf we can offer.
[04:13] Jordan Lee: ok let's dig into the 24h bench we agreed — what are the axes we want? Priya?
[04:18] Priya Malhotra: suggested axes: baseline hosted no-cache single-batch; hosted with cache at observed hit rates (20/30/40%); hosted with batching profiles (window 10/50ms, max batch 4/8/16); dedicated reserved 1x and 2x capacity with same cache/batch combos; quantization int8 vs fp16. we'll record tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latencies, and tokens per $ under our modeled pricing.
[04:42] Sofia Ruiz: and include a simulated traffic shape with your p95 spikes? we can provide real histogram.
[04:46] Priya Malhotra: yes please upload histograms — that will let us run a more realistic trace.
[04:50] Evelyn Park: what's the estimated time to run all that? you said 24h — is that per config?
[04:54] Priya Malhotra: ~24h total if we parallelize a bit, might be 36h worst-case. we'll prioritize the configs you care about.
[04:59] Marcus Chen: are there any tricky security or compliance items for the dedicated path we need to plan?
[05:04] Jordan Lee: for Private/dedicated we have VPC peering, KMS integration, audit logs — we'll send the security pack. for the POC dedicated setup we typically use encrypted disk and IAM roles; full SOC2 docs are in the security pack link we sent earlier.
[05:18] Evelyn Park: yes please send that again, the security folks will need to sign off before dedicated.
[05:22] Jordan Lee: will do.
[05:24] Priya Malhotra: small operational note on batching — if you need deterministic latency for certain calls, you can set a route with batch_size 1 and fast path and route the rest to batchers; that hybrid approach keeps UX snappy.
[05:36] Sofia Ruiz: that could work, we have a mix of synchronous search and async summarization flows.
[05:40] Jordan Lee: perfect. any other questions on tokens/sec/$ math?
[05:44] Marcus Chen: curious: how do you model the tokens/$ — is it purely runtime measured tokens divided by billed cost or do you include infra overhead?
[05:50] Priya Malhotra: for the POC we use runtime measured token generation and apply Redwood's list price for the model variant plus infra amortization for dedicated cases; for dedicated we include GPU hourly rate, storage, and orchestration overhead; we can show a line-item breakdown in the sheet.
[06:03] Evelyn Park: please show per-token breakdown and a 6-month projection for us.
[06:07] Jordan Lee: yes we'll add a 6-month projection with different adoption scenarios: low/medium/high traffic.
[06:12] Sofia Ruiz: what's the best way to measure cache hit-rate in our integration? we don't want to overcount.
[06:17] Priya Malhotra: instrument prefix hashes and track KV gets vs misses. we can share a small snippet for the instrumentation. also measure unique prefixes over time; that gives you the expected steady-state hit-rate.
[06:28] Marcus Chen: any gotchas around user-specific data — caching may be less effective if prompts include lots of user IDs.
[06:33] Priya Malhotra: yep — you can normalize user-specific tokens or separate routes; caching is best for shared system prompts and templated user messages.
[06:40] Evelyn Park: ok makes sense. I think the three next steps we discussed should cover it.
[06:44] Jordan Lee: to recap: Priya runs the extended bench and uploads the raw results + an annotated sheet; Jordan shares updated pricing with dedicated scenarios; Lunaris shares prompt set and traffic histograms. aim to reconvene after results are uploaded.
[06:58] Sofia Ruiz: thanks everyone, that works.
[07:00] Marcus Chen: thanks.
[07:02] Evelyn Park: thanks, bye.

Links/references mentioned: benchmark spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example.com/sheets/lunaris-bench-03-27), security pack (link: https://redwood.example.com/security/soc2-pack), instrumentation snippet (internal link).

End of transcript.
